payload.throughline: Choose the explanatory scale, compare stability and power lenses, and apply a gendered-power analysis without treating any lens as a value judgment.

learner_content_blocks: Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify the actor, institution, and outcome named in a social case; the frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite lesson.
Starting observation: An explanation says a student changes an answer after noticing classmates exchange doubtful looks. Which scale is primary?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: identify whether an explanation works mainly through face-to-face interaction or through institutions and broad social patterns, then state the consequence of that choice. The frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite handoff for this lesson.

A microsociological explanation centers interactions, meanings, roles, and small-group processes. A macrosociological explanation centers institutions, stratification, population patterns, and large-scale social organization.

Scale is not a verdict or a complete theory. A micro lens can reveal how a rule is enacted while omitting where the rule came from; a macro lens can reveal patterned constraints while omitting how people interpret them in an encounter.
Use a zoom control, not a scoreboard. Zoom in for interactional mechanisms; zoom out for structural mechanisms. After choosing, write one visible feature and one blind spot.

I locate the causal verb. If the explanation says people interpret a gesture, I choose micro. If it says an institutional funding rule distributes opportunity across regions, I choose macro. I do not decide by the number of people mentioned alone.
A school rule assigns students to tracks using a district-wide testing policy, while teachers communicate expectations differently within each track.
The district assignment rule is macro because it is institutional. The teacher-student expectation process is micro because it operates through interaction. One case can contain both scales.
Guided scale selection: underline the proposed mechanism, place it at a level, and name one adjacent level it leaves unexplained.
Less support: classify a fresh explanation by mechanism rather than by topic or group size.
On your own: state both the selected scale and its explanatory consequence.
Boundary: an explanation about one person can still invoke a macro institution, and an explanation about a large crowd can still focus on micro interactions.
Near exit: identify the operating scale in a familiar institution-and-interaction case.
Changed exit: read a nested-level diagram and determine which scale reveals the pattern and which process it omits.
Repair classification: replace the topic noun with the mechanism verb, then ask whether that mechanism occurs in an encounter or through a structural arrangement.
Fresh re-entry: classify a new mechanism with new actors and institutions.
Repair explanatory consequence: write one sentence beginning “This scale reveals…” and a second beginning “It does not by itself explain…”.
Fresh changed re-entry: select a scale and identify its blind spot in an unexposed nested case.
Recap: scale follows mechanism; micro foregrounds interaction, macro foregrounds structure, and each choice reveals some relations while omitting others.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify the institution, group interests, and observed stability or inequality in the case before selecting a lens.
Starting observation: An explanation says standardized schedules coordinate transportation, work, and school so institutions can operate together. Which lens is foregrounded?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: compare how functionalism and conflict theory explain the same institution without treating either lens as praise or blame. The frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite handoff for this lesson.
Functionalism asks how interdependent institutions or practices contribute to coordination, continuity, stability, or adaptation; it can also identify dysfunctions.
Conflict theory asks how unequal power and competition over resources shape institutions, whose interests are served, and how inequality is maintained or contested.
Use two columns on one case: FUNCTION/STABILITY asks what keeps the system operating; POWER/INEQUALITY asks who controls resources, who benefits, and who bears costs.

I hold the facts constant and change only the lens. For a credential rule, functionalism may predict standardized role sorting; conflict theory may predict advantages for groups that control access to credentials.
A city requires a costly license to operate a food stall. The rule standardizes inspections but excludes many low-capital vendors.
A functionalist explanation foregrounds coordination and safety standards. A conflict explanation foregrounds how the cost restricts market access and protects better-resourced operators.
Guided comparison: write one stability or function prediction and one power or inequality prediction for the same institution.
Less support: choose the lens whose premise matches a fresh explanation.
On your own: distinguish lens prediction from approval of the institution.
Boundary: functionalism does not claim every practice is beneficial, and conflict theory does not claim cooperation never occurs.
Near exit: identify which lens generated a case explanation.
Changed exit: derive contrasting predictions after an institution changes who controls a resource.
Repair lens selection: circle function, coordination, stability, power, resources, or inequality in the explanation and match the governing premise.
Fresh re-entry: identify the lens in a new institution case.
Repair prediction: hold the institution constant, then ask what each lens expects when coordination improves or resource control shifts.
Fresh changed re-entry: generate the lens-consistent prediction for an unexposed resource-control change.
Recap: functionalism foregrounds system contribution and stability; conflict theory foregrounds power, contested resources, and inequality.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify who holds decision power, who receives benefits, and who bears unpaid or hidden costs in the case.
Starting observation: A case shows one gender performs most unpaid care while another holds most household financial authority. Which question is most aligned with feminist theory?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: apply feminist theory to gendered power and inequality at introductory depth, focusing on institutions and social roles rather than advanced schools of theory. The frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite handoff for this lesson.
A feminist lens asks how gendered norms and power shape decision authority, paid and unpaid labor, resource access, status, and exposure to costs.
The analysis can operate across interactional and structural levels. A simple cost-and-benefit table helps reveal distribution, but no formal game-theory mathematics is required or authorized.
Use four arrows: who decides, who benefits, who performs the labor, and who bears the cost. Then ask which gendered rule or expectation connects them.
I do not stop at counting men and women. I identify the decision rule or norm, trace resources and burdens, and predict how changing that rule could alter inequality.
A workplace schedules promotion meetings after standard hours. Attendance is formally open, but employees carrying most evening caregiving are less able to attend.
A feminist analysis foregrounds how a formally neutral schedule interacts with gendered caregiving expectations to shape access to decision makers and advancement.
Guided power map: identify decision authority, resource access, labor, and burden, then connect them to the gendered arrangement.
Less support: choose the feminist-theory explanation from a fresh institutional case.
On your own: distinguish a power-and-inequality explanation from a simple count or personal-prejudice claim.
Boundary: a numerical gender difference alone does not identify its mechanism, and feminist theory is not limited to face-to-face bias.
Near exit: apply the lens to an explicit gendered division of labor and decision power.
Changed exit: predict how a policy that redistributes decision access or unpaid burden could alter the observed inequality.
Repair the power map: name one decision, one resource, one labor burden, and the gendered rule connecting them.
Fresh re-entry: apply the map to a new institution with different roles and resources.
Repair prediction: change only the stated gendered rule, then trace which access, burden, or authority relation should shift first.
Fresh changed re-entry: predict a bounded consequence of a new institutional change without claiming all inequality disappears.
Recap: feminist analysis traces gendered decision power, resources, roles, benefits, and burdens, then predicts bounded effects of changing those arrangements.
